details: Soviet state secrecy classification system: (1) Совершенно секретно / Sovershenno Sekretno (Top Secret): nuclear weapons; reactor design vulnerabilities; accident data; (2) Секретно / Sekretno (Secret): reactor operational data; radiation monitoring; nuclear city locations; (3) Для служебного пользования / Dlya sluzhebnogo polzovaniya (For official use only): routine operational data; (4) Не для печати / Ne dlya pechati (Not for publication): sensitive but not classified; (5) Открытые / Otkrytye (Open): published data; scientific papers; RBMK-1000 design: classified as 'Secret' from 1973-1992; specific classified information: (a) positive void coefficient magnitude (+4-8 pcm/%void); (b) graphite tip effect (+2-3β); (c) actual ORM minimum safe value; (d) Leningrad 1975 power surge accident; (e) Beloyarsk Unit 1 accident 1978; all nuclear accident data: automatically 'Top Secret' regardless of severity; KGB responsibility: ensure no leakage of nuclear facility information
chernobyl_application: RBMK operators' information access: operators trained on RBMK procedures WITHOUT being told: (1) actual magnitude of void coefficient; (2) that ORM minimum 15 was safety-critical (told it was operational guidance only; not safety limit); (3) that graphite tip effect existed; (4) prior accident history at other RBMK plants; Toptunov (age 25; reactor control engineer): had never seen void coefficient physics derivation; never told ORM=8 created dangerous condition; Dyatlov (deputy chief engineer): knew positive void coefficient existed but did not know the magnitude; believed coolant void effect manageable; institutional knowledge compartmentalization = direct cause of accident; comparison: US NRC requires ALL safety-significant reactor parameters in operator certification exams
source: Plokhy 2018 Chernobyl Ch.4; INSAG-7 1992 §5.2; Higginbotham 2019 Ch.14; nuclear_safety_culture_REAL.csv

details: Leningrad NPP Unit 1 accident 1975: RBMK-1000 (identical to Chernobyl); partial fuel channel rupture during power testing; power excursion detected; operators managed situation; damage: 1 fuel channel; no injuries; no public release; classified: 'Top Secret'; VNIIAES (All-Union Scientific Research Institute for Nuclear Power Plant Operation) internal report: documented the event; noted: positive void coefficient behavior contributed; recommended: review ORM minimum; recommendations: NOT implemented; not communicated to other RBMK plants; Chernobyl operators: never told about Leningrad 1975; Beloyarsk 1978: fuel channel rupture; steam release; fire; 1 worker died; classified; KURSK 1980: power instability event during startup; not disclosed; pattern: Soviet nuclear industry had 4-5 significant RBMK incidents 1973-1985 that were all classified; lessons NOT shared; Chernobyl = predictable consequence of serial classified near-miss failure
chernobyl_application: Had Leningrad 1975 not been classified: (1) Operators at all RBMK plants would have been retrained on void coefficient danger; (2) ORM minimum would have been formalized as safety limit (not operational guidance); (3) SCRAM system redesign (graphite tip problem known); (4) possibility: Chernobyl accident may have been prevented; this is the core lesson of INSAG-7 (1992): 'The direct cause was operating with too few control rods; but the fundamental cause was failure to communicate safety-critical information across the Soviet nuclear industry'; transparency = prerequisite for safety; secrecy = safety deficit; post-Chernobyl: Convention on Nuclear Safety (1994) Article 9 explicitly requires sharing of safety-significant information among nations

details: RBMK design flaw classification history: Positive void coefficient (+4-8 pcm/%void): known to reactor physicists since RBMK-1000 design stage (1969-1973); classified: (1) RBMK designers knew it was safety concern; (2) included in internal VNIIAES documents marked 'Secret'; (3) NOT included in operator training manuals (classified to protect from operators and outside parties); (4) NOT disclosed to IAEA (Soviet RBMK was presented as meeting IAEA safety standards; no mention of positive void coefficient); graphite tip effect: known since first RBMK-1000 startup tests 1973; documented in classified startup test reports; safety action required but not taken; ORM critical safety value: defined internally as 15 rods equivalent; NOT specified in operating regulations (regulations said 15 rods 'recommended' not minimum-required); gap between classified physics knowledge and unclassified operating procedures = accident root cause
chernobyl_application: Post-INSAG-7 (1992): IAEA publicly acknowledged that design characteristics of RBMK were safety-significant issues known before Chernobyl; Soviet nuclear engineers confirmed in interviews (Dollezhal; Alexandrov; and others): positive void coefficient was known, was considered acceptable, was NOT communicated to operators; WANO (World Association of Nuclear Operators) established 1989 in direct response to information isolation; peer review program: operators visit each other's plants; exchange operating experience (OE) including near-misses; OE sharing = formal mechanism to prevent Leningrad-1975-to-Chernobyl recurrence; Convention on Nuclear Safety 1994 Article 9: operators SHALL ensure all personnel have adequate training; implied: they must be told about safety-significant characteristics
